analysis.one_liner: Expands required advance notice of plant closings and layoffs to smaller firms and doubles employer penalties for violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have widened the federal WARN Act, which requires employers to warn workers before plant closings and mass layoffs. It would have covered employers with 50 or more workers instead of 100, triggered notice for closings affecting 25 workers instead of 500, covered part-time workers, and required notice to every affected employee personally. It also would have doubled the money employers owe when they skip notice, added interest, and let the Labor Department investigate complaints and sue on workers' behalf.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with roughly 50 to 500 employees, including part-time workers, who today get no legally required warning before losing their jobs. Workers at multi-site companies whose closings are spread across locations, and all laid-off workers, who could collect double back pay plus interest from employers that gave no notice. Workers without a union would now get individual written notice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at smaller firms facing layoffs

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the employer-size threshold from 100 to 50 employees and the layoff trigger from 500 (or 50 plus one-third of a site) to 25 employees, so smaller closings and smaller firms are covered [S2].
Closes loopholes: a company spreading cuts across many sites owes notice once 100 jobs are lost in total, and part-time employees count [S2][S3].

Sets a tiered notice window: 30 days for 25-49 affected workers, 60 days for 50-99, and 90 days for 100 or more, and requires written notice to each affected employee, not just a union representative [S2][S3].

Adds interest and liquidated damages equal to the back pay owed, and gives workers the choice of suing or filing a complaint with the Secretary of Labor, who must investigate and can sue on their behalf [S2][S3].
Requires employers to post notices explaining the law and how to file a complaint, with fines up to $100 per willful posting violation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially mid-sized firms between 50 and 499 workers that are currently exempt from the law. They would face new notice duties, compliance and posting costs, and up to double back pay plus interest in court or Labor Department actions if they close or lay off without warning.

drawbacks.text: The bill doubles employer liability and lets the Labor Department sue, which raises the cost of closing or downsizing and could push some employers toward preemptive cuts or restructuring to stay under thresholds [S2][S3].

The tiered thresholds create cliffs, so a closing affecting 24 workers triggers nothing while 25 triggers 30 days of pay liability, which rewards careful headcount management at workers' expense [S3].
The notice periods scale with size, so workers at the smallest covered firms get only 30 days of warning, which may be little time to find comparable work [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing permanent job loss, 30 to 90 days of warning plus double back pay against employers that skip notice is a substantial benefit, and the enforcement fix addresses a known weakness of the original law, where workers had to sue individually to collect. The costs fall on employers that have already decided to eliminate jobs, and the compliance burden is modest compared with the payroll costs of the shutdown itself. The cliff thresholds are a real design flaw, but the core trade-off strongly favors affected workers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee, which referred it to its Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee in November 1994, and the Congress ended in January 1995 with no markup, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Rep. William Ford of Michigan, the chairman of the House Education and Labor Committee, introduced the bill on March 17, 1994 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1][S5].
On November 14, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, the last action of record before the 103rd Congress expired on January 3, 1995 [S5][S1].
It never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would have owed 30-to-90-day notices and double back-pay liability for closings and layoffs at the 50-to-500-worker level are better off, since the stronger WARN rules never took effect. Workers at those firms are left with the original, narrower notice law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers exempt from expanded layoff notice rules

against.name: Employer trade associations
against.role: Business lobbies for small and mid-sized firms
against.what_they_did: Long opposed broadening WARN Act coverage and increasing employer liability for skipping layoff notice.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown exists; the sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats, and no Republicans appear anywhere in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have pulled these firms under the WARN Act for the first time, requiring advance notice of closings affecting 25 or more workers and exposing them to double back-pay liability plus interest. Their interest in avoiding notice obligations runs against workers' interest in warning before job loss.

Firms already covered would face the longer 90-day notice window, individual notice to every affected employee, and an aggregate rule that stops spreading cuts across sites to dodge the trigger. The added liability falls only on those that close or lay off without notice.
The bill would have created an administrative complaint process, subpoena authority, and authority to sue on behalf of workers, expanding the Department's enforcement role.
